bounds.domain: One PGlite backend; two client lifetimes with one finite Parse/Bind/Describe/Execute/Sync cycle each, or one simple-query peer; one optional explicit transaction on client 0, ending through COMMIT or ROLLBACK; one SQL error and one disconnect or raw exception; one bounded reset attempt. Optional server shutdown can close the remaining peer while waiting for owned recovery. Client 0 alone can stage one provisional write.
bounds.ownership: Each backend await has an active handler. Extended-cycle ownership starts before the first extended frame and survives until the owner's Sync; an ignored simple Query after SQL error cannot release it. Explicit transaction ownership can survive that Sync. Disconnect deactivates the client before clearing queued work. Recovery retains exclusive ownership through initial ROLLBACK, Sync, any required explicit-transaction ROLLBACK, and an idle acknowledgement. A raw backend exception or reset failure rejects work and leaves the backend unavailable.
bounds.progress: CleanupSettles assumes weak fairness of completion of an in-flight backend call, a recovery attempt, and release after an idle acknowledgement. ShutdownSettles also assumes weak fairness of shutdown completion after its owned detach task settles. Recovery may fail and leave the queue closed; stopped then means the listener closed with a cleanup error, not a clean backend. No fairness is assumed for client messages or request dispatch. A client that never sends Sync or disconnects can retain its cycle indefinitely.
bounds.effects: A successful Execute can leave one provisional write. Cleanup cannot publish a write orphaned before the client admitted Sync or COMMIT. An already-admitted commit may have an unknown successful outcome after disconnection; cancellation does not undo such a commit. The initial ROLLBACK precedes Sync to avoid committing an orphaned successful implicit transaction.

limitations: Each socket handler owns one connection lifetime. After detach starts it rejects attach without owning the supplied socket. The server creates a fresh handler for each connection; its queue retains no closed-client identity tombstones. Real-wire conformance checks retirement and a fresh client's continued use.
Messages are complete abstract frames, not arbitrary TCP bytes. The real-wire conformance owns framing, actual PostgreSQL responses, parameter values, and portal retention checks.

Named statement uniqueness, SQL parsing, every PostgreSQL message, multiple portals per client, unbounded queues, repeated client lifetimes, provider scheduling, and all application transaction isolation are outside these finite bounds. Close and Flush share the extended-cycle ownership boundary but are not separate modeled frames.

Backend acknowledgements abstract successful protocol reset. Real conformance must verify cleanup with disconnects before Sync, after Execute, and after SQL error; a model pass alone does not establish TypeScript or vendor-patch refinement.
No wall-clock deadline or unconditional client/request progress is proved. A failed reset requires the existing server/process restart boundary.

assumptions: An in-flight backend frame eventually completes or fails. Recovery attempts and acknowledged releases are weakly fair. Cleanup can end with a failed, closed queue; successful reset is not assumed. No client Sync, network delivery, or general request scheduling fairness is assumed.

The written cleanup fairness holds, and shutdown completion is weakly fair after owned detach tasks settle. Completion can report cleanup failure while closing the listener; it does not establish backend readiness.
No fairness is assumed. The checker must retain a loop that can leave a disconnected owner's cleanup pending indefinitely.
